dialogs.title: حوار — آخر يوم في المعهد
dialogs.intro: The last day of the semester. Ustaz Sameh is wrapping up the class, and Budi asks a question that has bothered him from the start.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: يا أستاذ، عندي سؤال بقالي شهور.
lines.id: Sir, I've had a question for months.
lines.literal: O teacher, at-me question it's-been-for-me months.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.id: Go ahead. Today the time is all yours.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أنا اتعلمت مصري. طيب الفصحى إيه لزومها؟
lines.baca: ana it‘allimt maṣri. ṭayyib il-fuṣ-ha ’ēh luzumha?

lines.text: سؤال كويس. بص: الفصحى بتتقرا، والعامية بتتقال.

lines.id: So newspapers and the news are all in Fusha?

lines.text: أيوه. والكتب والخطب والعقود. بس محدش بيتكلمها.

lines.literal: yes. and-the-books and-the-sermons and-the-contracts. but nobody he-speaks-it.

lines.text: عامية طبعاً. عشان كده الناس في كل البلاد بتفهم المصري.
lines.baca: ‘ammeyya ṭab‘an. ‘ashaan kida n-naas fi kull il-bilaad bitifham il-maṣri.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: طيب أتعلم فصحى دلوقتي ولا بعدين؟
lines.baca: ṭayyib at‘allim fuṣ-ha dilwa’ti walla ba‘dēn?

lines.literal: OK I-learn Fusha now or later?

lines.text: دلوقتي حتلاقيها سهلة. عندك الكلمات وعندك الودن.

lines.id: Now you'll find it easy. You have the words and you have the ear.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: But I'm afraid of mixing the two up.

lines.speaker: أستاذ سامح:
lines.text: كل المصريين بيخلطوا! ده مش غلط، ده طبيعي.

lines.id: All Egyptians mix them! It's not a mistake, it's natural.

lines.text: ارتحت خلاص. شكراً على كل حاجة يا أستاذ.
lines.baca: irtaht khalaaṣ. shukran ‘ala kull haaga ya ustaaz.

lines.text: ده واجب. وماتنساش تتكلم كل يوم، ولو مع نفسك.

lines.id: It was my duty. And don't forget to speak every day, even if only to yourself.

lines.text: إن شاء الله. أشوفك السنة الجاية.

notes: **This division of labor between Fusha and ammiyya is called diglossia**, and it lives across the whole Arab world. The key point: Fusha is for what is **written and read aloud**, ammiyya for what is **spoken**. No native speaker chats in Fusha at home.
**The word محدش means "nobody", a blend of ما، حد، ش.** Its relatives: مافيش حاجة (nothing at all), عمري ما (never in my life), ولا واحد (not a single one).

**The phrase عشان kida means "that's why", and عشان on its own covers two meanings**: "because" and "so that". عشان تعبان (because I'm tired), عشان أفهم (so that I understand). Context tells them apart, and the long form is علشان.

**The form بتتقرا is the Egyptian passive**, made by adding اتـ in front of the verb: قرا becomes اتقرا (was read), كتب becomes اتكتب (was written), عمل becomes اتعمل (was made). It's simple and works for almost every verb.
**The word غلط means "wrong, mistake", and it works as both noun and adjective.** ده غلط (that's wrong), عملت غلط (I made a mistake), غلطان (the person who's mistaken).

**The phrase ولو مع نفسك carries serious advice.** Talking to yourself out loud is one of the cheapest and most powerful ways to keep a foreign language alive, and almost everyone skips it because it feels silly.

grammars.title: One paragraph, two languages
body: Compare the same sentences in Fusha and in Egyptian. Everything you've learned over twenty units is summed up in this table.
after: Notice that the Egyptian column is almost always **shorter**. Spoken language wears away what it doesn't need, and case endings (i'raab) are the first to go, since word order already carries their meaning.

Notice too that the basic vocabulary is the same: كتاب، طالب، أشرب، أذهب. What differs is just the thirty most common words and the whole grammar toolkit — and that toolkit is what you now have in hand.
If you go on to Fusha, there are three things to add: case endings, question words that move to the front, and about five different negation words. That's it. You already have the rest.

grammars.title: Franco-Arab: Egyptian in Latin letters
body: Egyptians write Egyptian on their phones in Latin letters and numbers, and the system has been well established for two decades. Without it, you can't read half of everyday conversation.
after: The system was born when phones couldn't type Arabic letters, and it survives because it's quick to type. Young Egyptians use it on WhatsApp and Instagram; older people tend to go back to Arabic script.
You **don't need to write in this system**, but you do need to read it. Lines like *ana geet* or *enta fen ya 3am* will pop up on your screen all the time.

blocks.text: Everyday messages are written in Egyptian, while formal letters — job applications, letters to government offices — are written in Fusha. The table below gives a frame for both.

The right-hand column is in Fusha on purpose, and that's no slip in this book: Egyptian formal letters simply aren't written in ammiyya. You don't need to compose one yourself at A1, but knowing the shape tells you which one you're reading.

blocks.title: A complete message in Egyptian
items: Opening and greeting: أهلاً يا منى، إزيك؟ عامل إيه؟
Body: كنت عايز أشكرك على العزومة إمبارح. الأكل كان تحفة وماما بتاعتك تسلم إيديها.
Inviting back: المرة الجاية عندي أنا، إن شاء الله. قوليلي إمتى يناسبك.

blocks.text: What you have now is a complete framework. What you don't have yet is mileage, and that can only be built through your ears and mouth, not on the page.

blocks.text: If you can only pick one of the six, take the fifth. Egyptian is a spoken language before it is a written one, and one hour of real conversation moves you further than ten hours of reading alone.

items: You thank someone for yesterday's dinner invitation.
You praise the host's cooking to her son.
You invite them back for next time.
You ask to be told when a good time would be.
